sections.heading: Time Complexity
sections.text:
Measures how the number of operations grows as the input size (n) increases.
Focuses on the algorithm's efficiency rather than its actual running time.

sections.heading: Space Complexity
sections.text:
Measures how much additional memory an algorithm uses as the input size (n) increases.
Includes variables, data structures, recursion, and temporary storage used during execution.

sections.heading: Time Complexity
sections.text:
Describes how the number of operations changes as the input size (n) grows.
Used to compare the efficiency of algorithms.
Independent of hardware, programming language, or processor speed.
Example:
Reading an array of numbers is an example of O(n) or linear time because the elements in the array affects the amount of steps or operations it takes linearly.
int arr[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7};int arr_len = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]);for (int i = 0; i < arr_len; i++){    printf("%d ", arr[i]);}
n = 7
The loop does 7 iterations.
Amount of steps is the same as amount of elements.
Thus this is O(n)

sections.heading: Big-O Notation
sections.text:
Big-O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's time or space complexity, showing how its resource usage grows as the input size (n) increases.
Describes the growth rate.
Focuses on how an algorithm scales.

sections.heading: Asymptotic Notations
sections.text: Asymptotic notations are mathematical languages used to describe the execution time or space complexity of an algorithm relative to its input size. They allow programmers to analyze the efficiency of code by filtering out hardware-specific details and constant factors, focusing entirely on how the resource requirements scale as the input size grows toward infinity.

sections.heading: Big-O Notation (Asymptotic Upper Bound)
sections.text:
Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound. It guarantees that an algorithm will never run worse than a certain rate, but it is allowed to run much better. It represents a loose or inclusive limit.
It guarantees that an algorithm will never run worse than a certain rate, but it is allowed to run much better. It represents a loose or inclusive limit.

sections.heading: Small-o Notation
sections.text:
Small o (or little-o) is a mathematical tool used in asymptotic analysis to describe the relationship between functions, indicating that one function grows or decays strictly faster than another. Unlike Big O, which represents a "less than or equal to" relationship, little-o represents a strict "less than" relationship.
Little-o is a strict upper bound. It states that f(n) grows strictly slower than g(n). The two functions can never grow at the same rate; as n goes to infinity, g(n) completely dwarfs f(n).

sections.heading: Comparing Big-O and little-o
sections.text:
The easiest way to tell them apart is by comparing them to elementary school inequality symbols:
Big-O (O) acts exactly like <= (Less than or equal to). It represents a standard loose upper bound.
Little-o (o) acts exactly like < (Strictly less than). It represents a strict upper bound.

sections.heading: Asymptotic Lower Bounds: Big Omega (Ω) & little omega (ω)
path: Asymptotic Lower Bounds: Big Omega (Ω) & little omega (ω)
sections.text: Michael Litang

sections.heading: The Asymptotic Notation Family
sections.text:
Notation | Bound Type | Description
-------- | ---------- | -----------
O (Big O) | Upper bound | f(n) grows no faster than g(n). "At most this much."
Ω (Big Omega) | Lower bound | f(n) grows at least as fast as g(n). "At least this much."
Θ (Big Theta) | Tight bound | f(n) grows exactly as fast as g(n). "Exactly this much."

sections.heading: What Is Big Omega (Ω)?
sections.text:
The lower bound.
Ω(g(n)) describes functions that grow at least as fast as g(n), once n is large enough. It describes the best-case running time of an algorithm.
Analogy: "Your time is Ω(10 minutes)" means you will never finish faster than 10 minutes — you might take 10, 15, or 20, but never less. It's a floor you can't go below.

sections.heading: Formal Definition: Big Omega
sections.text:
f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that f(n) ≥ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
c > 0 — A fixed positive scaling constant, chosen once, stays fixed.
n₀ > 0 — The threshold after which the inequality always holds.
≥ (allowed) — f(n) may equal c·g(n); a tie still counts as satisfying Ω.

sections.heading: Quick Check (Big Omega Example)
sections.text:
f(n) = 5n + 3 is Ω(n) — pick c = 5 and n₀ = 1, then just plug in n
n | f(n) = 5n + 3 | c·g(n) = 5n
--- | ------------- | -----------
1 | 8 | 5
2 | 13 | 10
3 | 18 | 15
5 | 28 | 25
10 | 53 | 50
Notice: as n grows, f(n) stays on or above c·g(n) every single time — that's exactly what Ω(n) guarantees.

sections.heading: What Is little omega (ω)?
sections.text:
The strict lower bound.
ω(g(n)) is the stricter sibling of Big Omega. f(n) must grow strictly faster than g(n) — a tie is never allowed.
Analogy: "Your time is ω(5 minutes)" means you finish meaningfully slower than 5 minutes, and the gap only grows as the race gets longer. Tying at exactly 5 is never allowed.

sections.heading: Formal Definition: Little Omega
sections.text:
f(n) = ω(g(n)) if for every positive constant c, there exists n₀ such that f(n) > c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
'>' not '≥' — Strictly greater than; equality never satisfies little omega.
for EVERY c — Must hold for all possible positive constants, not just one you pick.
No tie allowed — f(n) and g(n) can never share the same growth rate.

sections.heading: Example (Little Omega)
sections.text:
f(n) = n² is ω(n) — try c = 10, find where n² finally passes 10n
n | f(n) = n² | c·g(n) = 10n | f(n) > c·g(n)?
--- | --------- | ------------ | --------------
8 | 64 | 80 | No
9 | 81 | 90 | No
10 | 100 | 100 | No (tie)
11 | 121 | 110 | Yes
15 | 225 | 150 | Yes
20 | 400 | 200 | Yes
Once n ≥ 11 = n₀, f(n) is always strictly greater — and it only pulls further ahead. That threshold is exactly what little omega needs.

sections.heading: Ω vs ω — Side by Side
path: Ω vs ω — Side by Side
sections.text:
Notation | Condition | Symbol | Equality allowed?
-------- | --------- | ------ | -----------------
Big Omega (Ω) | f(n) ≥ c·g(n) | ≥ (greater than or equal) | Yes
little omega (ω) | f(n) > c·g(n) | > (strictly greater than) | No
Easiest way to remember:
Big Omega (Ω) behaves like "≥" — ties are okay.
little omega (ω) behaves like ">" — no ties allowed.

sections.heading: Big Theta (Θ)
sections.text:
Big Theta is a way to describe the exact asymptotic growth rate of an algorithm's running time or memory usage. It tells us that an algorithm grows at the same rate as a given function, within constant factors, as the input size becomes very large.
Big Theta means the algorithm's performance is both an upper bound and a lower bound.

sections.heading: The Big Theta Notation (Formal Definition)
sections.text:
Assuming f(n) and g(n) are non-negative functions.
f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if and only if c1 · g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2 · g(n) for all values of n ≥ n0 and c1, c2, and n0 are constants.
f(n) = Θ(g(n)) = g(n) is the asymptotic of f(n)

sections.heading: What & Why
sections.text:
Definition: Predicting the Time (CPU operations) and Space (memory) an algorithm needs as input size (n) grows.
The Goal: Measuring the rate of growth to compare efficiency objectively, independent of hardware or programming language.

sections.heading: The Core Tools
sections.text:
Scenarios: Worst-Case (standard ceiling), Average-Case (expected), and Best-Case (floor).
Asymptotic Bounds:
(O), (Ω), (Θ) — Upper, Lower, and Tight bounds
(o), (ω) — Strict Upper and Strict Lower bounds

sections.heading: What is a Recurrence Relation?
sections.text:
A recurrence relation is a mathematical expression that defines a sequence in terms of its previous terms.
In the context of algorithmic analysis, it is often used to model the time complexity of recursive algorithms.

sections.heading: General Form
sections.text:
aₙ = f(aₙ₋₁, aₙ₋₂, ..., aₙ₋ₖ)
Breakdown of the notation:
a — The name of the sequence (just like calling a function f).
n — The position or index of the element in the sequence (1st, 2nd, 3rd, ... nth).
aₙ — The value at the specific nth position.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: The main purpose of a recurrence relation is to break down large, complex problems into simpler, smaller chunks until they reach a base case.

sections.heading: Its Core Purposes
sections.text:
Analyze Code: Measures the speed and memory usage of recursive software algorithms.
Optimize Software: Breaks problems into reusable sub-steps to save processing time.
Model Trends: Tracks step-by-step changes in population growth or financial compound interest.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.text:
The Fibonacci Sequence: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2), where F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1. Each number is the sum of the two preceding ones.
Compound Interest: Aₙ = Aₙ₋₁ * (1 + r), where Aₙ is the current amount, Aₙ₋₁ is the principal, and r is the interest rate.

sections.heading: The 4 Solving Methods
sections.text:
Iteration Method
Substitution Method
Recursion Tree
Master Theorem

sections.heading: 1. Iteration Method (Expansion Method)
sections.text: The Iteration Method (also called the Expansion Method) solves a recurrence by repeatedly replacing the recursive term until the base case is reached.

sections.heading: Parts of a Recurrence Relation
sections.text:
Example Problem: T(n) = T(n-1) + 2, T(1) = 4
Recursive Function — T(n): The value we want to determine.
Recursive Term — T(n - 1): The previous value that the current term depends on.
Non-recursive Part — +2: The constant or function added at each step.
Base Case (Initial Condition) — T(1) = 4.

sections.heading: Goal of the Iteration Method
sections.text:
The goal of the iteration method is to eliminate the recursive calls by repeatedly expanding the recurrence until reaching the base case.
Specifically, it aims to:
Convert a recursive equation into a closed-form equation.
Express T(n) directly in terms of n.
Avoid repeated recursion.
Make analyzing an algorithm's running time easier.
Instead of repeatedly computing T(5) = T(4)+2, T(4) = T(3)+2, ... we obtain the direct formula T(n) = 2n + 2.

sections.heading: Example Problem: T(n) = T(n-1) + 5, T(3) = 12
sections.text:
Step 1: Set up
Given: T(n) = T(n-1) + 5
Base case: T(3) = 12
Step 2: Find T(n-1)
Replace "n" with "n-1":
T(n-1) = T((n-1)-1) + 5
Simplify:
T(n-1) = T(n-2) + 5
Step 3: Substitute into the original equation
Original equation: T(n) = T(n-1) + 5, and we have T(n-1) = T(n-2) + 5.
Substitute:
T(n) = (T(n-2) + 5) + 5
Simplify:
T(n) = T(n-2) + 10
Step 4: Find T(n-2)
T(n-2) = T((n-2)-1) + 5  →  T(n-2) = T(n-3) + 5
Substitute back: T(n-2) = T(n-3) + 10, and T(n) = T(n-2) + 5, so:
T(n) = (T(n-3) + 5) + 10  →  T(n) = T(n-3) + 15
Step 5: Observe the Pattern
From the substitutions: T(n) = T(n-2) + 10, T(n) = T(n-3) + 15.
The pattern is:
T(n) = T(n-k) + 5k
Step 6: Use the Base Case
The base case is T(3) = 12. To reach the base case: n - k = 3.
Solve for k:
k = n - 3
Step 7: Substitute k
Replace k in the pattern:
T(n) = T(n - (n-3)) + 5(n-3)
Simplify:
T(n) = T(3) + 5(n-3)
Step 8: Use the Base Case Value
Since T(3) = 12, substitute it:
T(n) = 12 + 5(n-3)
Expand:
T(n) = 12 + 5n - 15
Simplify:
T(n) = 5n - 3
Final answer: T(n) = 5n - 3
Verification
Check the base case: T(3) = 5(3) - 3 = 15 - 3 = 12 ✓ (matches T(3) = 12)

sections.heading: 2. Substitution Method ("Guess and Prove")
sections.text: The Substitution Method is a technique used to find the time complexity of recursive algorithms by expanding the recurrence relation, identifying a pattern, and then proving the result using mathematical induction.

sections.heading: In Simpler Terms
sections.text:
A formal algebraic way to solve recurrence relations.
It does not find an answer from scratch — it proves a suspect guilty.
The Two Steps:
Guess: Predict the form of the solution (using intuition or recursion tree).
Prove: Use mathematical induction to show the guess is 100% correct.

sections.heading: The Inductive Rule
sections.text:
The Logic Flow:
Step 1 (Assumption): Assume our guess works for all smaller sub-problems (like T(k) where k < n).
Step 2 (Substitution): Substitute that assumption directly into the original equation formula.
Step 3 (The Goal): Show that the algebra balances out, proving it works for the whole problem T(n).

sections.heading: Key Concepts
sections.text:
Recursion → The Code: A programming technique where a function calls itself.
Recurrence → The Math: A mathematical equation that describes or measures the runtime of a recursive algorithm (e.g., T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn).
Big O Notation (O): Represents the upper bound or worst-case running time of an algorithm as the input size n grows.
Small c vs. Big C:
Small c: A fixed constant given in the original problem (the cost of work per element outside recursion).
Big C: A constant multiplier we choose in our guess to make the upper bound proof work, T(n) ≤ C · n log n.
Strong Induction: A form of induction where we assume the statement holds for all smaller values.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn
sections.text:
Target: Show that T(n) ≤ C · n log n, or T(n) = O(n log n).
Understanding the Parts of a Recurrence Relation
T(n) — Total execution time for input size n
2 — Number of recursive sub-problems
n/2 — Size of each sub-problem (halving the data)
cn — Extra work done outside recursion (e.g., merging)
Step 1: Make a Guess
Formulating the Inductive Hypothesis: We guess that the time complexity is O(n log n).
Mathematical Definition: We need to prove that T(n) ≤ C * n log n.
Why O(n log n)? By definition of Big-O this means T(n) ≤ C * n log n for some constant C > 0. O(n log n) is log-linear time — slightly worse than linear, but much faster than n² (e.g., merge sort).
Step 2: Inductive Step
Rule of Induction: If the guess works for n, it must work for smaller sizes like n/2 (since n/2 < n). We treat n as an input slot — in mathematical induction, we are trying to prove that the rule holds for any input size.
Substitute n/2 into every n in our guess formula:
T(n/2) ≤ C * (n/2) log (n/2)
Step 3: The Substitution
Start with the original recurrence:
T(n) = 2 * T(n/2) + cn
Replace T(n/2) with our Step 2 expression:
T(n) ≤ 2 * [C * (n/2) log (n/2)] + cn
Note: The 2 outside is the original multiplier attached to the sub-problems.
Step 4: Algebraic Simplification
The multiplier 2 cancels out the fraction n/2:
T(n) ≤ 2 * [C * (n/2) log (n/2)] + cn
Simplified:
T(n) ≤ C * n log (n/2) + cn
Step 5: Logarithm Rules & Distribution
Log Quotient Rule: log(a/b) = log(a) - log(b).
So log₂(n/2) = log₂(n) - log₂(2) = log(n) - 1  (since log₂(2) = 1).
Substitute back:
T(n) ≤ C * n * [log(n) - 1] + cn
Distribute C*n:
T(n) ≤ C * n log n - C * n + cn
Group terms:
T(n) ≤ C * n log n - (C - c)n
Step 6: Proving the Inequality
What we have: T(n) ≤ C * n log n - (C-c)n.
What we want: T(n) ≤ C * n log n.
Condition: The extra piece -(C-c)n must be negative or zero, i.e. C - c ≥ 0 → C ≥ c.
As long as we pick constant C ≥ c, we are subtracting a positive number, making the whole expression smaller than C * n log n.
Conclusion — Proof Complete!
Since T(n) ≤ C * n log n - (C-c)n ≤ C * n log n holds true for any C ≥ c, we have T(n) ≤ C * n log n.
Therefore, by mathematical induction:
T(n) = O(n log n)

sections.heading: 3. Recursion Tree
sections.text: A recursion tree is a diagram used in algorithm analysis to visualize how a recursive algorithm breaks a problem into smaller subproblems. Each node in the tree represents a recursive function call, and each branch represents another recursive call made by that function.

sections.heading: Components of a Recursion Tree
sections.text:
Root Node — Represents the initial function call or the original problem.
Internal Nodes — Represent recursive calls that continue dividing the problem into smaller subproblems.
Branches — Show the relationship between a function call and the recursive calls it creates.
Leaf Nodes — Represent the base cases where recursion ends and no further recursive calls are made.

sections.heading: Example: Cost per Level
sections.text:
Level 0:                    cn                          -> Cost = cn
/    \
Level 1:            c(n/2)      c(n/2)                 -> Cost = cn/2 + cn/2 = cn
/   \        /    \
Level 2:      c(n/4) ...   ...  c(n/4)                 -> Cost = 4 * c(n/4) = cn
/                        \
Level log2(n): T(1)  T(1)  T(1) ... T(1)               -> Cost = n * T(1) = O(n)

sections.heading: 4. Master Theorem
sections.text:
The Master Theorem is a tool used to solve recurrence relations that arise in the analysis of divide-and-conquer algorithms. The theorem gives asymptotic bounds on T(n) in terms of standard notations like Θ, O, and Ω. The Master Theorem provides a systematic way of solving recurrence relations of the following form:
T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n),   where a ≥ 1 and b > 1
n is the size of the problem
a ≥ 1 is the number of subproblems
n/b is the size of each subproblem (b > 1)
f(n) is the cost of work done outside the recursive calls (dividing the problem and combining results)

sections.heading: Why We Compare Two Things
sections.text:
n^(log_b a) — work from all sub-problems combined
f(n) — extra work outside the recursive calls
Whichever grows faster tends to control the total time

sections.heading: The Three Cases of the Master Theorem
path: The Three Cases of the Master Theorem
sections.text:
Case 1: Recursive side wins
Condition: f(n) is polynomially smaller than n^(log_b a)
Result: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a))
Case 2: A tie
Condition: f(n) grows at the same rate as n^(log_b a)
Result: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n)
Case 3: Outside work wins
Condition: f(n) is polynomially bigger than n^(log_b a)
Result: T(n) = Θ(f(n))

sections.heading: Worked Examples
sections.text:
Case 1 Example: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n
a = 4, b = 2, f(n) = n
n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂4) = n²
Compare: f(n) = n and n^(log_b a) = n². Since n² grows faster, this is Case 1.
Result: T(n) = Θ(n²)
Case 2 Example: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = 1
n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂1) = n⁰ = 1
Compare: f(n) = 1 and n^(log_b a) = 1. They are the same, so this is Case 2.
Result: T(n) = Θ(log n)
Case 3 Example: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n²
a = 3, b = 2, f(n) = n²
n^(log_b a) = n^(log₂3) ≈ n^1.58
Compare: f(n) = n² and n^(log_b a) ≈ n^1.58. Since n² grows faster, this is Case 3.
Result: T(n) = Θ(n²)

sections.heading: CSP 111 - Algorithm and Complexity
sections.text: Group 4 | Module 4: Algorithm Design Techniques

sections.heading: What & Why
sections.text:
Definition: An equation that defines a sequence or problem using its previous terms.
Real-World Analogy: Dominoes falling down, or compound interest growing year by year.
Predicts Performance: Predicts CPU time and memory usage as data size grows.

sections.heading: 4 Ways to Solve Recurrence Relations
sections.text:
Iteration Method
Substitution Method
Recursion Tree Method
Master Theorem

sections.heading: Core Definition & Process
sections.text:
A problem-solving technique that breaks one large problem into smaller problems, solves each one using recursion, then combines the solutions to form the final answer.
01. DIVIDE: Break the original problem into smaller subproblems.
02. CONQUER: Solve each smaller subproblem, usually using recursion (until reaching the base case).
03. COMBINE: Put the smaller solutions together into the final answer.

sections.heading: Example 1: Finding the Maximum Number
sections.text:
Problem: Find the largest value in the list [8, 3, 5, 2, 7, 4].
Divide: Split [8, 3, 5, 2, 7, 4] into [8, 3, 5] and [2, 7, 4]. Further divide until single-element base cases: [8], [3], [5], [2], [7], [4].
Conquer: A single-element list is already solved.
Combine: Compare maximums of sublists: max(8, 3, 5) = 8, max(2, 7, 4) = 7. Final comparison max(8, 7) = 8.
Final Answer: 8

sections.heading: Example 2: Merge Sort
sections.text:
Problem: Put the numbers [8, 3, 5, 2, 7, 4] in order from smallest to largest.
Divide: Split array in half repeatedly until single elements are reached: [8], [3], [5] and [2], [7], [4].
Conquer: A single element has nothing left to order—it is naturally sorted.
Combine: Merge sorted pieces: [3, 5, 8] and [2, 4, 7] → [2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8].

sections.heading: Complexity
sections.text:
Finding Maximum: O(n) - Every element is examined once; work grows linearly with input size.
Merge Sort: O(n log n) - Splitting in half repeatedly requires far fewer comparisons than checking every pair.

sections.heading: Greedy AlgorithmsCore Concepts
sections.text:
Greedy Choice Property: Each local best choice is assumed to lead towards the global optimum.
Optimal Substructure: An overall optimal solution is formed from optimal subproblems.
Efficiency: Typically linear or logarithmic time complexity.
Limitation: Not all problems can be solved optimally with greedy methods.

sections.heading: How Greedy Algorithms Work
sections.text:
1. Start with the initial problem state.
2. Evaluate all available options at the current step.
3. Pick the best option right now (largest coin, shortest edge, etc.) without regard for future consequences.
4. Repeat until the problem is completely solved.
5. Result may be optimal or near-optimal depending on problem structure.

sections.heading: Coin Changing Problem
sections.text:
Problem: Make change for 'n' units using the minimum number of coins.
Denominations: Available coin denominations C = {100, 25, 10, 15, 1}.
Algorithm Pseudocode:
MAKE-CHANGE(n)  C <- {100, 25, 10, 15, 1}  S <- {} (solution set)  sum <- 0  WHILE sum < n DO    x <- largest item in C such that sum + x <= n    IF no such item THEN RETURN 'No Solution'    S <- S union {x}    sum <- sum + x  END WHILE  RETURN S

sections.heading: Traveling Salesman Problem (Greedy Failure Example)
sections.text:
A salesman starts at city A and visits every city using the nearest unvisited city rule (greedy selection).
Greedy Choice: Greedy path: A -> B -> D -> B -> C -> E (Cost = 16).
Actual Optimal Path: A -> D -> B -> C -> E (Cost = 14).
Conclusion: Demonstrates that greedy choices do not always guarantee a globally optimal path.

sections.heading: Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
sections.text:
Kruskal's Algorithm: Greedily adds the lowest-weight edge that connects distinct subtrees until all vertices are connected.
Prim's Algorithm: Starts with a single vertex and greedily expands by adding the minimum-weight edge connecting the tree to a new vertex.

sections.heading: Huffman Encoding
sections.text: A greedy algorithm for optimal prefix coding. It repeatedly picks the two nodes with the lowest frequencies and combines them until a complete binary code tree is constructed.

sections.heading: Advantages & Disadvantages
sections.text:
Advantages: Easier to implement, requires fewer computing resources, and executes very fast.
Disadvantages: Does not always reach the global optimum solution (though sub-optimal results are often good approximations).

sections.heading: Dynamic Programming
sections.text:
What is Dynamic Programming?
Dynamic Programming (DP) solves complex problems by breaking them into smaller sub-problems, solving each sub-problem once, and saving their answers in memory (a table or array) to avoid redundant calculations.

sections.heading: The Real-World Analogy (2 x 2 x 2)
sections.text:
Step 1: If written '2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2', you calculate it to get 32.
Step 2: If another 'x 2' is added at the end, you instantly say 64 because you remembered 32 instead of recalculating from scratch. That is DP.
When to Use Dynamic Programming?
Overlapping Subproblems: The problem requires repeating the exact same calculation multiple times.
Optimal Substructure: The optimal solution to the problem can be constructed easily from optimal solutions of its subproblems.
Remember & Reuse: Create a 'notepad' (array or hash map) to store solved subproblem answers for instant lookup.

sections.heading: Implementation Approaches
sections.text:
Top-Down Approach: 'Start from top, write notes as you go.' Solves subproblems recursively and caches results (Memoization).
Bottom-Up Approach: 'Build from the ground up.' Solves base cases first and fills a lookup table iteratively (Tabulation).

sections.heading: Fibonacci Example
sections.text:
Naive Recursion: Requires calculating Fib(3) twice, Fib(2) three times, resulting in exponential O(2^n) work.
DP Approach: Calculates Fib(3) once, stores it in a table, reducing time complexity to O(n).

sections.heading: Backtracking
sections.text:
What is Backtracking?
Backtracking is a systematic, trial-and-error algorithm design technique. It attempts to build a solution incrementally, one step at a time. If a choice leads to an invalid state or dead end, the algorithm backtracks by removing the last choice and trying an alternative path.

sections.heading: How Backtracking Works (Step-by-Step)
sections.text:
1. Initialize: Start with an empty or partial solution.
2. Make Choice: Add one possible option.
3. Check Validity: Verify if the current partial solution remains valid.
4. Continue: Proceed to build the rest of the solution.
5. Backtrack: If dead end is reached, undo the last choice (backtrack).
6. Repeat: Explore alternative options until a valid solution is found or all possibilities are exhausted.

sections.heading: Time Complexity in Backtracking
sections.text:
O(n): Linear time—searching through a flat list of n elements.
O(2^n): Exponential time—each decision point has multiple choices (e.g., n switches with 2 choices each leads to 2^n possibilities).

sections.heading: Example: 3-Digit Password Combination (Target: 231)
sections.text:
Step 1: Try 1 -> 11, 12, 13 (Dead ends -> Backtrack)
Step 2: Try 2 -> 21, 22 (Dead ends -> Backtrack)
Step 3: Try 2 -> 23 -> 231 (Success! Password Found)

sections.heading: 7. Branch and Bound Algorithm
sections.text:
What is Branch and Bound?
Branch and Bound is an algorithm design technique used for solving combinatorial optimization problems (e.g., 0/1 Knapsack, Traveling Salesman, Job Scheduling). It systematically searches the state-space tree while using calculated bounds to prune unproductive branches.

sections.heading: Three Core Operations
sections.text:
BRANCH: Divide the problem/node into smaller subproblems (child nodes). E.g., decide whether to include or exclude an item.
BOUND: Calculate the best possible estimate (upper/lower bound) for subproblems along a branch.
PRUNE: Discard/stop expanding branches whose estimated bound cannot beat the current best solution.

sections.heading: Steps in Branch & Bound
sections.text:
1. Start with the root node (original problem state).
2. Compute its initial bound.
3. Select a promising node to expand.
4. Generate child nodes (Branching).
5. Compute bounds for the new child nodes.
6. Prune/discard nodes whose bounds are worse than the current best known solution.
7. Repeat until all promising nodes are explored.
8. Output the best feasible solution.

sections.heading: 0/1 Knapsack Example (Branch & Bound)
sections.text:
Knapsack Parameters: Maximum Capacity W = 12
Item | Weight (w) | Value (v) | Value/Weight Ratio | Upper Bound Formula
---- | ---------- | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------
Item 1 | 3 | $30 | 10 | UB = V + (W - w)*(v_{i+1} / w_{i+1})
Item 2 | 4 | $28 | 7 | UB = 30 + (12-3)*7 = 93
Item 3 | 5 | $25 | 5 | UB = 58 + (12-7)*5 = 83
Item 4 | 6 | $18 | 3 | UB = Optimal bounded value

sections.heading: 1. Breadth-First Search (BFS)
sections.text:
Breadth First Search (BFS) is a graph traversal algorithm that starts from a source node and explores the graph level by level. First, it visits all nodes directly adjacent to the source. Then, it moves on to visit the adjacent nodes of those nodes, and this process continues until all reachable nodes are visited.
Time complexity: O(V + E)

sections.heading: How BFS Works
sections.text:
Choose a starting node.
Mark it as visited.
Add it to the queue.
Remove the first node from the queue.
Visit all of its unvisited neighboring nodes and add them to the queue.
Repeat until the queue is empty.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
Sample graph (undirected), connected as follows:
Edge | Edge | Edge
---- | ---- | ----
A – B | A – C | A – D
B – E | B – F | C – G
C – H | D – H | 
Starting a BFS at node A (visiting neighbors in alphabetical order):
Queue: [A] → visit A, enqueue B, C, DQueue: [B, C, D] → visit B, enqueue E, FQueue: [C, D, E, F] → visit C, enqueue G, HQueue: [D, E, F, G, H] → visit D (no new neighbors)Queue: [E, F, G, H] → visit E (no new neighbors)Queue: [F, G, H] → visit F (no new neighbors)Queue: [G, H] → visit G (no new neighbors)Queue: [H] → visit H (no new neighbors)Traversal order: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H

sections.heading: 2. Depth-First Search (DFS)
sections.text: DFS is a graph/tree traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.

sections.heading: How DFS Works
sections.text:
Start at a chosen node (the root, or any starting point).
Visit that node, mark it as visited.
Recursively visit an unvisited neighbor.
Keep going deeper until you hit a node with no unvisited neighbors.
Backtrack to the previous node and try its next unvisited neighbor.
Repeat until every reachable node has been visited.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
Sample graph (undirected), connected as follows:
Edge | Edge | Edge
---- | ---- | ----
A – B | D – G | H – I
B – C | D – E | E – F
A – D | C – H | G – F
Starting a DFS at node A (visiting neighbors in alphabetical order):
Visit A → visit B → visit C → visit H → visit I  (dead end, backtrack)Backtrack to A → visit D → visit E → visit F → visit G  (dead end, backtrack — all visited)Traversal order: A, B, C, H, I, D, E, F, G

sections.heading: 3. Topological Sorting
sections.text:
The process of arranging the vertices (nodes) of a directed graph in a specific order based on their dependencies.
It follows the rule that if there is an edge A → B, A must come before B in the ordering.
It is only possible in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), which is a graph with no cycles.

sections.heading: How Topological Sorting Works
sections.text:
Identify the vertices that have no incoming edges.
Choose one of these vertices and add it to the ordering.
Remove the chosen vertex and its outgoing edges.
Repeat the process until all vertices are arranged.
The resulting sequence is the topological order.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
Sample directed acyclic graph (DAG):
Edge | Edge | Edge
---- | ---- | ----
5 → 2 | 5 → 0 | 4 → 0
4 → 1 | 2 → 3 | 3 → 1
Applying the algorithm (repeatedly picking a vertex with no remaining incoming edges):
Step | Vertex Chosen | Why It Qualifies | Ordering So Far
---- | ------------- | ---------------- | ---------------
1 | 4 | No incoming edges to start with | 4
2 | 5 | No incoming edges to start with | 4, 5
3 | 2 | Its only incoming edge (5→2) is gone | 4, 5, 2
4 | 0 | Both incoming edges (5→0, 4→0) are gone | 4, 5, 2, 0
5 | 3 | Its incoming edge (2→3) is gone | 4, 5, 2, 0, 3
6 | 1 | Both incoming edges (4→1, 3→1) are gone | 4, 5, 2, 0, 3, 1
Topological order: 4, 5, 2, 0, 3, 1
Note: a topological order is not always unique. Since 4 and 5 have no dependency between them, swapping their positions (e.g. 5, 4, 2, 0, 3, 1) is also a valid ordering.

sections.heading: 4. Dijkstra's Algorithm
sections.text:
Developed by Edsger Wybe Dijkstra.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a starting node to every other node in a weighted graph (where edges have costs/distances, not just connections).
Note: This is different from DFS/BFS, which just explore connectivity — Dijkstra's tracks cost, not just reachability.

sections.heading: The Core Idea: Greedy + Priority Queue
path: The Core Idea: Greedy + Priority Queue
sections.text: Always expand outward from whichever unvisited node currently has the smallest known distance. This greedy choice guarantees correctness as long as edge weights are non-negative.

sections.heading: Relaxation Formula
sections.text:
if dist[u] + weight(u, v) < dist[v]:    dist[v] = dist[u] + weight(u, v)
In words: new candidate distance to v = dist[u] + weight(u, v). If it beats the current best-known distance to v, update it.

sections.heading: Algorithm Steps
sections.text:
Set distance to the start node = 0, all others = infinity.
Put all nodes in a priority queue, ranked by current known distance.
Pop the node with the smallest distance. Mark it finalized.
For each neighbor, relax the edge.
Repeat until the queue is empty.

sections.heading: Example: A to C
sections.text:
Graph edges and weights:
Edge | Weight | Edge | Weight
---- | ------ | ---- | ------
A – F | 3 | B – E | 1
A – B | 2 | B – C | 7
A – D | 5 | D – E | 1
F – B | 4 | D – G | 1
E – G | 3 | G – C | 4
E – C | 3 |  | 
Running Dijkstra from source A:
Node | Cost | Previous
---- | ---- | --------
A | 0 | —
B | 2 | A
C | 6 | E
D | 4 | E
E | 3 | B
F | 3 | A
G | 5 | D
Shortest path from A to C:  A → B → E → C  (total cost = 6)

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a start node to every other node in a weighted graph by greedily expanding the closest unvisited node first — using a priority queue for efficiency — which is only correct when all edge weights are non-negative.

sections.heading: 5. Bellman-Ford Algorithm
sections.text:
Developed by Richard Bellman and Lester Ford Jr.
The Bellman-Ford Algorithm is a graph algorithm used to find the shortest path from a starting vertex to other vertices in a weighted graph.
Finds the shortest path
Starts from a source vertex
Works with weighted graphs
Can handle negative edge weights
Can detect negative weight cycles

sections.heading: Key Terms
sections.text:
Vertex – a point or node in the graph
Edge – connection between two vertices
Weight – value assigned to an edge
Example: A ----4----> B   (A and B are vertices, the arrow is an edge, 4 is the weight.)

sections.heading: Relaxation
sections.text:
Checking if a shorter path exists and updating the distance if necessary.
if distance[u] + weight < distance[v]:    distance[v] = distance[u] + weight
u = starting/source vertex of the edge; v = destination vertex of the edge; weight = the cost of going from u to v.

sections.heading: How Bellman-Ford Works
sections.text:
Initialize distances.
Set source = 0.
Set other vertices = infinity (∞).
Relax all edges V − 1 times.
Check for a negative weight cycle.

sections.heading: Example Graph
sections.text:
Edges and weights (note the negative edge B → C):
Edge | From → To | Weight
---- | --------- | ------
1 | A → B | 4
2 | A → C | 5
3 | B → C | −3
4 | C → D | 2
5 | A → D | 10

sections.heading: Finding the Initial Distances
sections.text:
Source vertex = A. Set A's distance to 0, and all others to infinity (∞).
Vertex | Initial Distance
------ | ----------------
A | 0
B | ∞
C | ∞
D | ∞
After relaxing every edge V − 1 = 3 times, the shortest distances from source A are:
Vertex | Shortest Distance | Path from A
------ | ----------------- | -----------
A | 0 | A (cost = 0)
B | 4 | A → B (cost = 4)
C | 1 | A → B → C (cost = 1)
D | 3 | A → B → C → D (cost = 3)

sections.heading: Negative Weight Cycle
sections.text:
Example: A → B = 2, B → C = −4, C → A = 1
Total: 2 + (−4) + 1 = −1  →  a negative total means a negative weight cycle exists.

sections.heading: Pseudocode
sections.text: BellmanFord(Graph, Source)  Set source distance = 0  Set other distances = infinity  Repeat V - 1 times:    For every edge:      Relax the edge  Check every edge again  If distance can still decrease:    Negative cycle exists

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Bellman-Ford finds the shortest paths from a single source, handles negative edge weights, and detects negative weight cycles.

sections.heading: 6. Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
sections.text:
Developed by Robert W. Floyd, Stephen Warshall, and Bernard Roy.
The Floyd-Warshall Algorithm is a graph algorithm used to find the shortest paths between every pair of vertices in a weighted graph.
Finds the shortest path between all pairs of vertices
Works with weighted graphs
Can handle negative edge weights
Can detect negative weight cycles
Uses a dynamic programming approach
Continuously checks if going through another vertex gives a shorter path

sections.heading: Key Idea
sections.text: Repeatedly checks whether going through another vertex provides a shorter path between two vertices.

sections.heading: Formula
sections.text:
dist[i][j] = min( dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] )
i = the starting vertex, j = the destination vertex, k = the intermediate vertex being checked as a possible shortcut.

sections.heading: Worked Example
sections.text:
Example graph: A → B = 4, B → C = 2, C → A = 11.  (∞ = no direct path, 0 = distance to self)
Initial distance matrix D⁰ (direct edge weights only):
From \ To | A | B | C
--------- | --- | --- | ---
A | 0 | 4 | ∞
B | ∞ | 0 | 2
C | 11 | ∞ | 0
Final distance matrix, after checking every vertex as a possible intermediate stop:
From \ To | A | B | C
--------- | --- | --- | ---
A | 0 | 4 | 6
B | 13 | 0 | 2
C | 11 | 15 | 0

sections.heading: 7. Prim's Algorithm
sections.text: Associated with Vojtěch Jarník, Robert C. Prim, and Edsger W. Dijkstra.

sections.heading: What Is a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)?
path: What Is a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)?
sections.text:
A Minimum Spanning Tree is a tree that:
Connects all vertices
Has no cycles
Uses exactly V − 1 edges
Has the minimum possible total weight

sections.heading: Finding the Minimum Spanning Tree
sections.text:
Prim's algorithm is a greedy algorithm used to connect all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight.
Key idea: Start from one vertex and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects to an unvisited vertex.

sections.heading: How Prim's Algorithm Works
sections.text:
Choose a starting vertex.
Look at all edges connected to the current tree.
Choose the lowest-weight edge that connects to an unvisited vertex.
Add that edge and vertex to the tree.
Repeat until all vertices are connected.
Key rule: Always choose the cheapest edge that expands the tree.

sections.heading: 8. Kruskal's Algorithm
sections.text:
Developed by Joseph Kruskal.
Kruskal's Algorithm is a method used to find the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a weighted graph.
In simple words: it connects all the nodes using the lowest possible total edge weight, without creating a cycle.
Key idea: Choose the smallest edge first, but do not create a cycle.

sections.heading: How Kruskal's Algorithm Works
sections.text:
List all edges in the graph.
Sort the edges from smallest to largest weight.
Select the smallest edge.
Check for a cycle.
If it does not create a cycle, add it to the MST.
Continue until all vertices are connected.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
Graph edges and weights (vertices A–G):
Edge | Weight | Edge | Weight
---- | ------ | ---- | ------
B – D | 5 | G – F | 12
A – B | 6 | A – G | 15
C – F | 9 | C – D | 17
F – E | 10 | D – E | 22
B – C | 11 | G – C | 25

Edge | Weight | Creates a Cycle? | Added to MST?
---- | ------ | ---------------- | -------------
B – D | 5 | No | Yes
A – B | 6 | No | Yes
C – F | 9 | No | Yes
F – E | 10 | No | Yes
B – C | 11 | No | Yes
G – F | 12 | No | Yes
A – G | 15 | Yes | No
C – D | 17 | Yes | No
D – E | 22 | Yes | No
G – C | 25 | Yes | No
MST edges: B–D, A–B, C–F, F–E, B–C, G–F.  Total weight = 5 + 6 + 9 + 10 + 11 + 12 = 53

A quick review of last module's topics before diving into this one:
Breadth-First Search (BFS) — A graph traversal algorithm that starts from a source node and explores level by level, visiting all direct neighbors before moving further out. Time complexity: O(V + E).
Depth-First Search (DFS) — A traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking to try the next unvisited neighbor.
Topological Sorting — Arranges the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that for every edge A to B, A comes before B in the ordering.
Dijkstra's Algorithm — Finds the shortest path from a starting node to every other node in a weighted graph by greedily expanding the closest unvisited node, using a priority queue. Requires non-negative edge weights.
Bellman-Ford Algorithm — Finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all others in a weighted graph, and unlike Dijkstra's, it can handle negative edge weights and detect negative weight cycles.
Floyd-Warshall Algorithm — A dynamic programming algorithm that finds the shortest paths between every pair of vertices by repeatedly checking whether routing through another vertex gives a shorter path.
Prim's Algorithm — A greedy algorithm for finding a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST): starting from one vertex, it repeatedly adds the cheapest edge that connects to an unvisited vertex.
Kruskal's Algorithm — Also finds a Minimum Spanning Tree, but by sorting all edges by weight and adding the smallest edge at each step as long as it doesn't create a cycle.

sections.heading: What Is Maximum Flow?
sections.text: Maximum flow is an algorithmic problem that calculates the greatest possible total amount of traffic, data, or liquid that can move from a starting Source to a final Sink through a network of connected pathways, where every pathway has a strict capacity limit.

sections.heading: The Two Core Rules
sections.text:
Capacity Constraint — The flow on any edge cannot exceed that edge's defined capacity.
Flow Conservation — For every intermediate node (any node that is not the Source or the Sink), the total flow entering the node must equal the total flow leaving it. Matter or data cannot magically appear or disappear at internal points.

sections.heading: Core Concepts & Key Rules
sections.text:
Source (S) — Starting node where flow originates.
Sink (T) — Final destination node where all flow must arrive.
Capacity — The maximum physical limit an edge can carry.
Flow — The actual amount currently moving through an edge.
Example: in the path S → A → T, where S → A has capacity 10 and A → T has capacity 7, the flow along that path is 7 — the narrowest ('bottleneck') link limits how much can get through.
Source, sink, capacity, and flow along a simple path.

sections.heading: The Ford-Fulkerson Algorithm
sections.text:
The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm is a greedy strategy used to calculate the maximum flow in a network graph from a Source (S) to a Sink (T). Instead of guessing all paths at once, it uses an iterative greedy approach powered by residual graphs:
Augmenting Path: search for any valid path from Source to Sink with remaining capacity.
Bottleneck: identify the smallest capacity link on that path and push that amount of flow through.
Add Reverse Edges (undo mechanism): create backward residual edges so future iterations can cancel or reroute sub-optimal flow choices.
Walking through the example graph below (S, A, B, C, T):
Path S → A → T: bottleneck = min(10, 7) = 7. S→A residual becomes 3, A→T becomes saturated (0). Running total: 7.
Path S → B → T: bottleneck = min(10, 10) = 10. Both S→B and B→T become saturated. Running total: 7 + 10 = 17.
No paths remain: both A→T and B→T have 0 forward capacity left, so no further augmenting paths exist.
Final state: Max Flow = 17 (edge A→T carries 7/7, edge B→T carries 10/10).

sections.heading: Calculating Max Flow — Example
sections.text:
A larger network to practice on, with source S, sink T, and intermediate nodes A, B, and C:
Practice network: S→A (8), S→B (10), A→C (4), A→B (3), B→C (5), B→T (7), C→T (6).

sections.heading: Takeaways
sections.text:
Maximum Flow — the highest total volume of flow that can move from source to sink.
Two Core Rules — Capacity Constraint and Flow Conservation.
Ford-Fulkerson Algorithm — the standard method for calculating maximum flow.
3-Step Loop — the algorithm repeatedly finds an augmenting path, pushes the bottleneck flow, and updates residual capacities.
Path Choice Flexibility — different valid path choices can still arrive at the same correct maximum flow.

sections.heading: String Matching
sections.text:
String matching is the process of comparing a string of characters with another string or a specified pattern to determine whether they are identical, or whether one occurs within the other. For example, searching for "cat" in "The cat is sleeping" is string matching, because the pattern "cat" occurs within the larger text.
Three classic algorithms accomplish this, each with different trade-offs:
Naive (Brute-Force) Search
Rabin-Karp Algorithm (Rolling Hash)
Boyer-Moore Algorithm

sections.heading: The Running Example
sections.text: Throughout this section, the same running example is used: searching for the pattern "CONT" (4 characters) inside the text "FLOODCONTROL" (12 characters).

sections.heading: 1. Naive (Brute-Force) Search
sections.text:
The naive search slides the pattern across the main text one position at a time, comparing each letter until it finds a full match or runs out of positions to try.
Naive search sliding window: comparing "CONT" against the text at the matching position — every character checks out.
Complexity:
Mechanism: at every text shift i (0 to n−m), compare the pattern P against the substring T[i...i+m−1].
Time complexity: O((n − m + 1) × m), which simplifies to O(n × m) in the worst case.
Best case: O(n), when mismatches are found immediately at each position.
Worst case: O(n × m), which happens with highly repetitive text and patterns.
Limitations: it discards all information gathered during partial matches, so each new position starts comparisons completely from scratch.

sections.heading: 2. Rabin-Karp Algorithm (Rolling Hash)
sections.text:
Rabin-Karp converts string comparison into numerical comparison using modular arithmetic:
Map characters to numbers using base d, where d represents the alphabet size.
Compute the hash value h(P) for the pattern and h(T) for the current text window, both modulo a prime number q.
Slide the window one position at a time, updating the hash value in constant time using a rolling hash formula instead of recomputing it from scratch.
Only when the hash values match does the algorithm perform a direct character-by-character check, to rule out hash collisions.
Rolling hash values matching (81 = 81) confirm the suspect pattern is found at index 5 to 8.
Complexity:
Average case: O(n + m).
Worst case: O(n × m), due to frequent hash collisions.
Best used for: searching for multiple patterns simultaneously, such as in plagiarism detection.

sections.heading: 3. Boyer-Moore Algorithm
sections.text:
Boyer-Moore compares characters from right to left, starting from position m−1 down to 0 within the current search window, and uses mismatches as clues to skip large sections of text at once — rather than sliding one space at a time.
Two heuristics drive the skipping:
Bad Character Rule: when a mismatch occurs at T[i] = c, the pattern is shifted right so that the rightmost occurrence of c in the pattern realigns with position i.
Good Suffix Shift: uses previously-matched suffixes to skip ahead even further.
The algorithm shifts by whichever of the two rules suggests the larger jump. A precomputed Bad Match Table stores the shift distance for each character.
Bad Match Table and the final located match — the suspect pattern "TOTN" found at index 8 to 11.
Complexity:
Best case: O(n / m), sub-linear, because the algorithm can skip large sections of the text.
Worst case: O(n × m), though this is rare in practice with a well-built bad match table.
